new_entries.name: Exogenous activity halt
causal_chain: An external, non-financial shock (pandemic, natural disaster, war) forces a sudden, economy-wide stop in normal activity that no market participant caused or can quickly reverse
Demand and supply collapse simultaneously across many sectors as movement, gathering, and production are curtailed at once
Cash flows evaporate for exposed firms while fixed obligations continue, triggering a scramble for liquidity and a sharp asset-price drawdown
The shock's path depends on the exogenous event and the policy response, not on the usual internal build-up of leverage or valuation excess
Recovery timing is set by the external event's resolution and the scale/speed of fiscal-monetary backstop, and can be far faster or slower than a normal financial-cycle recession

historical_instances.case: https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating -- COVID-19 recession: NBER dated the peak February 2020 and trough April 2020; the downturn was 'so great and so widely diffused throughout the economy that, even if it proved to be quite brief,' it was classified a recession (S&P 500 fell ~34% peak-to-trough in Feb-Mar 2020)
historical_instances.source: https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating -- NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee, US business-cycle chronology

instance.case: PENDING-MAC-VERIFICATION -- 2021-22 post-pandemic inflation: pandemic supply-chain disruptions plus an energy price surge (amplified by the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war) passed through into broad consumer prices, with US CPI peaking near 9.1% year-over-year in June 2022
instance.source: https://www.bls.gov/cpi/ -- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index (Jun-2022 CPI ~9.1% YoY) [sandbox fetch not attempted for a data landing page; routed to citation_check.sh]

instance.case: PENDING-MAC-VERIFICATION -- 2022-23 Fed hiking cycle: the FOMC raised the federal funds target ~525bp from near zero (Mar 2022) to ~5.25-5.50% by mid-2023 -- the fastest tightening in four decades -- to break entrenched inflation, with rate-sensitive sectors (housing, long-duration equities) contracting first
instance.source: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm -- Federal Reserve, Open Market Operations / policy rate actions 2022-2023 [routed to citation_check.sh]
